newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. envoy hopes to close Iraq's weapons file soon.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy hopes to close Iraq's weapons file soon.

text.p: United Nations arms envoy Richard Butler on Monday expressed hope that the U.N. would be able to close Iraq's weapons files "as soon as possible", Baghdad television reported.

It said Butler, an Australian who took over as chairman of the United Nations Special Commission (UNSCOM) on Iraq this month, told reporters that he wanted to start a new phase with Iraq and with new determination to settle all issues.
"He (Butler) expressed that he was entrused with submitting a credible report to the Security Council on what had been achieved of (Iraq's) prohibited weapons," the television said.
Butler replaced Sweden's Rolf Ekeus who led UNSCOM, the U.N body in charge of dismantling Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, since its inception soon after the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.

UNSCOM must certify that Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations can lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
"We will try to start a new phase (with Iraq)...and with new determination to deal with all issues," Butler said.
Butler, on his first visit to Baghdad, said he would be fair in his new assignment in Iraq and he would be "instructed by no one".
He said he would meet Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz on Wednesday to discuss with him how to "achieve the work" of the Special Commission in Iraq.
Few hours before Butler arrived in Baghdad Iraqi newspapers urged him to open a new page with Baghdad.
"...What Iraq sincerely wants and seeks is that the Special Commission with its new chairman opens a new page with it," newspaper of thr ruling Baath party al-Thawra said in a front- page editorial.
"It is in the interest of Iraq that its ties with the Special Commission are stable and it is confirmed that Iraq will cooperate with it," it said.

Last month Iraq barred U.N. inspectors from entering three sensitive sites, prompting the Security Council to issue a resolution warning Iraq it would face further sanctions if it blocked U.N. inspectors.
